title: Ottawa Street South rezoning and tenant displacement
subtitle: Access Without Fear policy, Duke Street and King Street East developments, planning fees, and Rotary Plaza naming.
overview: Council's main debate was a rezoning for 1257-1265 Ottawa Street South, which would allow a 20-unit stacked townhouse project to replace two houses that are being used as rooming accommodation for about a dozen tenants. Council first rejected a deferral {{vote:m3}}, then approved the rezoning {{vote:m4}}. Changes include an eight-foot fence and a staff review of on-site parking, including compact spaces, through site plan approval.

Council also approved the Access Without Fear Policy {{vote:m1}}, so people without immigration status can use city services without being asked for status or reported. Approvals went to a Knossos Housing Corporation development on Duke Street and Madison Avenue North {{vote:m2}}, a mixed-use project at 4220 King Street East {{vote:m5}}, and one at 1251 King Street East {{vote:m15}}. Council also set 2023 planning and committee of adjustment fees {{vote:m17}}.

A councillor gave notice of a motion for January 30, 2023 asking staff to report on infill displacement and best practices. Council also approved $93,821.29 in tax adjustments {{vote:m19}}. After closed session, it approved a café lease at 198 King Street West and a land swap with the Waterloo Catholic District School Board involving Kinzie Park. The city also renamed the Duke Street Plaza as Rotary Plaza.

decisions.detail: Council approved the zoning changes for the 20-unit project, with an eight-foot fence and a direction that staff review on-site parking, including compact spaces, through site plan approval {{vote:m4}}.
A motion to defer to January 30, 2023, to seek tenant relocation details and ask the Region for a traffic study, was lost {{vote:m3}}.
Council approved a policy that lets people without immigration status use city services without being asked for status or reported to other governments {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.item: 206-210 Duke Street and Madison Avenue North
decisions.detail: Council adopted an Official Plan amendment and approved zoning for a Knossos Housing Corporation multiple residential development, with the plan forwarded to the Region for approval {{vote:m2}}.
Council adopted an Official Plan amendment and approved zoning for a high-intensity mixed-use project, with a floor space ratio of 5.2 {{vote:m5}}.
Council approved the 2023 planning application fees, two engineering fees and committee of adjustment fees {{vote:m17}}.
Council declared 300 Kinzie Avenue surplus and authorized sale of it to the Waterloo Catholic District School Board, with purchase of part of 50 Thaler Avenue to relocate the park {{vote:m22}}.
Council delegated hearings on development charge complaints to the Finance and Corporate Services Committee under the process in the staff report {{vote:m9}}.

debate: Delegates opposed to the Ottawa Street rezoning raised traffic safety, including recent collisions near the site and the lack of a traffic impact study. They also raised limited parking on neighbouring streets, privacy, and the size of the project compared with the lot.

Housing and homelessness advocates said the tenants pay rents that are hard to find elsewhere. They said first and last month's rent and moving costs are not enough, and asked for more support, a right to return, or deeply affordable units. A housing advocacy group supported this type of density but opposed displacement without adequate compensation.

Staff said the Planning Act framework does not let the city require tenant compensation or affordable units through a zoning amendment. They said a traffic study was not warranted, the application was past the 90-day appeal point, and extra height would need an Official Plan amendment.

Several councillors said refusing the application would likely lead to a loss at the Ontario Land Tribunal, with legal costs and possible damages under Bill 23, and chose to approve it while pursuing advocacy. Others voted against, citing the displacement of tenants paying affordable rents.

On the Access Without Fear policy, staff said the city does not collect immigration status data, so the policy aims to build awareness and trust. Staff described staff training first, then a public awareness campaign, focused on community centres.
